articles.title: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet
articles.summary: The purchase has sparked outrage over its cost as many Ghanaians struggle with rising cost of living.
articles.body:
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.

The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.

But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.

The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.

Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations?

Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.

Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.

The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.

While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.

Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.

"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.

He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.

Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.

The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.

"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.

But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.

Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.

Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.

"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.

He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.

"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.

Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.

Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.

He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.

"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.

The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.

But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".

"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.

He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.

The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.

The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.

Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.

Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.

"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.

articles.title: A luxury handbag designer sued King Charles’ charity for £6m after a fundraiser collapsed; the High Court rejected her main claims but allowed a £25,000 expense claim against FareShare.
articles.summary: A planned fundraising dinner in London was supposed to bring together fashion, celebrity contacts and a cause closely associated with King Charles.
articles.body: A planned fundraising dinner in London was supposed to bring together fashion, celebrity contacts and a cause closely associated with King Charles. For Amanda Navaian, founder of sustainable luxury handbag label Marici London, the proposed collaboration was also an opportunity to introduce her brand to a wider audience. The plans involved a T-shirt fundraising campaign, with 50% of the retail value intended for the Coronation Food Project and the remaining 50% allocated to the operation and expansion of the business, alongside a fundraising dinner at an upmarket restaurant.But the partnership never reached the launch stage. As reported by the Royal Courts of Justice, London, after the event was cancelled in July 2024, Navaian took legal action against the King Charles III Charitable Fund and two other defendants, seeking £6m in compensation. The High Court has now rejected most of her claims.How Navaian brought sustainable fashion into a royal charity initiativeNavaian founded House of Marici in 2020, developing a luxury handbag business around sustainability and ethical fashion. The brand promotes alternatives to conventional leather, with an emphasis on plant-based materials and avoiding plastic. With around two decades of experience in marketing and brand development, she saw the Coronation Food Project as an opportunity to bring her business and charitable interests together.Her interest in the initiative was also connected to her admiration for King Charles and his environmental values. In April 2024, she approached Dori Dana-Haeri, who chaired the development committee for the project, with a proposal for a fundraising T-shirt collection. A fundraising dinner based on a "Conscious Dining" concept was planned at CLAP in Knightsbridge, with ultra-high-net-worth guests expected to make donations to attend and Dame Martina Milburn expected to deliver a speech.The court heard that Navaian had also been introduced to the King during the course of the project and had shown him one of her sustainable handbags. She believed the proposed collaboration would extend beyond a single fundraising event, bringing her label into contact with people in the charity, business, fashion and celebrity worlds.How a disputed Zoom conversation shaped the £6m court battleAccording to The Independent, the dispute largely turned on a Zoom meeting held on 29 April 2024. Navaian maintained that an oral agreement had been reached during the discussion involving herself, Dana-Haeri and Dame Martina Milburn, co-chair of the Coronation Food Project. According to her case, the conversation gave her the go-ahead to begin organising the fundraising initiative.She argued that the arrangement involved more than permission to produce charity T-shirts and organise a dinner. Her account included expectations that Marici would receive recognition as a social enterprise supporting the project, alongside introductions and associations that could improve its standing among ethical consumers, investors, journalists and celebrities.The defendants disputed that a legally binding agreement had been made. Their position was that the discussions did not create contractual obligations of the kind Navaian later described. The High Court ultimately accepted that there was no reasonably arguable basis for treating the April meeting as a binding contract.In his ruling, Mr Justice Mansfield said several of the alleged terms appeared to reflect what Navaian hoped the partnership would achieve rather than commitments that had actually been agreed. He also questioned how the defendants could have guaranteed that the project would raise millions or that the handbag company would gain greater recognition through the association.The last-minute restaurant dispute that brought the fundraiser to a haltPreparations continued through the following weeks, but the relationship between Navaian and the restaurant became a separate source of difficulty. CLAP London contacted the parties in July 2024 to say the dinner would be postponed indefinitely. The event had been expected to take place the following day.The disagreement concerned arrangements for supplying alcohol to guests. Navaian later told FareShare that the restaurant had withdrawn following a dispute over who would manage that provision. During the court proceedings, the judge also referred to an exchange in which she had called those running CLAP "thieves" during a telephone conversation with a charity representative.The restaurant's decision became important to the legal case because Navaian alleged that the defendants had contributed to the cancellation. She argued that the charities had communicated with CLAP in a way that encouraged it to abandon the event.However, the judge found no proper basis for concluding that the defendants had instructed the restaurant to cancel or had persuaded it to do so. He also said there was no sufficient legal foundation for the allegation that they had acted unlawfully to damage her business.Celebrity contacts and the business losses claimed by NavaianNavaian told the court that she had invested considerable time and effort in preparing for the launch. She had approached friends and people in her professional network, including stylist and socialite Olivia Buckingham, who was expected to help curate the guest list. She believed the dinner would attract celebrities and influencers, while the proposed T-shirt initiative would give the partnership a wider public profile.She described the cancellation as a turning point for the business, saying the people involved in the project wanted explanations after the plans fell apart. In her account, the consequences extended beyond the loss of one event.Navaian argued that the cancellation had cost her a significant commercial opportunity, claiming that the launch could have generated substantial sales for her business. She also said the experience had affected her ability to continue working for a considerable period. Her claim included allegations of breach of contract, misrepresentation and unlawful interference with economic relations. Together with Marici London Ltd, she sought £6m from the King Charles III Charitable Fund, FareShare and Dana-Haeri.The defendants' barrister, Andrew McLeod, challenged the basis of the compensation figure, arguing that the claimed losses were speculative and insufficiently detailed. The judge's decision meant that the bulk of the claimed losses would not proceed to a full trial.High Court rejects the main allegations against the royal charityIn his ruling, Mr Justice Mansfield found that the alleged oral agreement from the April 2024 Zoom meeting had no realistic prospect of being established as a binding contract. The discussions were at an early stage, with further agreements still expected, and the responsibilities described in Navaian's claim lacked the detail needed to create enforceable obligations.The judge also rejected the claims of misrepresentation and unlawful interference with economic relations. He found no proper basis for suggesting that the defendants had instructed CLAP London to cancel the dinner or persuaded the restaurant to do so. The court also found insufficient grounds to conclude that the defendants had intended to damage Navaian's business.The judge expressly criticised FareShare's argument that an itemised invoice had not been supplied. He said it was unclear whether an itemised invoice was actually required under the reimbursement agreement and questioned why the invoice already submitted was deficient. FareShare had acknowledged a separate agreement to reimburse qualifying expenses of up to £25,000. The judge criticised the charity's explanation for withholding the payment, observing that it was not clear whether an itemised invoice was actually required under the agreement.Navaian and Marici London Ltd were given 28 days to file and serve an amended claim against FareShare, limited to qualifying expenses of up to £25,000, exclusive of VAT. If they failed to meet the deadline, the remaining claim would be struck out.The defendants had also made an open offer to pay the £25,000. The judgment therefore brought the main £6m legal battle to an end in the defendants' favour, while leaving the limited reimbursement issue subject to further action.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court reporting and the reported High Court ruling. The Times of India has not independently verified the claims made by the parties.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: South Africa stopped five baobabs from being shipped to Georgia; after more than three months stranded in Durban, the trees are now heading 900 km to a sanctuary
articles.summary: Five giant baobab trees are on their way to a sanctuary after being saved from illegal export to Georgia. Learn about the rescue efforts and the importance of preserving these ancient giants.
articles.body: Five giant baobab trees have finally left a warehouse yard in Durban, South Africa. They started a 900 km road trip to a sanctuary in the Timbavati Private Nature Reserve, sitting between Mpumalanga and Limpopo, on 11 November, according to a report by the Daily Maverick. The trees had spent more than three months lying on their sides after officials halted their export to the country of Georgia. The same report described them as thirsty and shrunken, but still alive. For once, a story about trees in trouble has a hopeful plot twist.How five ancient trees ended up in DurbanThe baobabs were uprooted in the Lephalale region of the Limpopo province. They were then transported over 800 km to the port city of Durban. Officials stopped them at the Africa Global Logistics warehouse on 17 July 2026. A spokesperson from the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) told Daily Maverick that the exporter could not show a licence. The department said the required procedures had not been followed. According to the reports, the baobabs were supposed to be used in a landscaping project in Georgia. A criminal investigation had been launched. Estimates of their age differ, but some reports put the trees at 200 to 300 years old. Plant specialist Geoff Nichols, working from photographs, suggested they could be more than 50 years old if taken from the wild. Each one is believed to weigh between 17 and 30 tonnes. For more than three months they lay on hot paving as the legal questions played out.The law and the science behind the fussBaobabs are protected in South Africa. A government notice under the National Forests Act sets out the rules. It states that no one may cut, disturb, damage, or destroy a protected tree. It also includes removing, transporting, exporting or even buying one without the right licence. Breaking the rules constitutes a criminal offence under the Act. Baobabs are also protected in terms of Limpopo’s own environmental legislation, the department added, and no permit was obtained in terms of that legislation.Baobabs may look unbreakable, but they face real threats. Nature Plants published a study titled ‘The demise of the largest and oldest African baobabs,’ which analysed over 60 of the biggest and oldest African baobabs. The study described the African baobab as one of the biggest and longest-living flowering trees. The authors found that, over the course of 12 years, nine of the 13 oldest trees died or their oldest stems collapsed. Five of the six largest met the same fate. The researchers said the causes were still unclear, but they suspected changing climate conditions might have been a factor. The study didn't consider moving trees, but it showed why every old baobab is important.What happens next and why it matters The trees were lifted into giant load trucks by a huge crane in Durban. The project, known as Operation Baobab, was initiated by ecologist Dr Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation. Timbavati Private Nature Reserve offered to sponsor loading, transportation, and replanting costs. There is, however, no guarantee that the trees will thrive once replanted. Meanwhile, there has been progress on the legal front as well. Follow-up coverage by Daily Maverick showed that the department turned down a licence after the event, and the exporter's appeal was dismissed on 27 October. The exporter is due to return to the Durban Magistrates’ Court in January 2027. Lawyers for the exporter claim that the trees came from private gardens with permission. The department has not identified the buyer yet. Some reports link the trees to a billionaire's private garden in Georgia, but the rumours are unconfirmed. Venter argues that the rescue goes beyond these five trees since losing them would have sent the wrong message to the world about South African conservation.Big money can make nature into a shopping list. This case shows that rules still count and people are paying attention. A similar row broke out in Kenya in 2022 concerning right baobabs from Kilifi County, also bound for Georgia. If readers around the world care about the planet, this piece of story might feel like a small win worth rooting for. The real test, however, will come months after these ancient giants are planted.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Council to caretake Alpamare waterpark until sale completes
articles.summary: Alpamare at Scarborough's North Bay was taken over by North Yorkshire Council earlier this month.
articles.body:
A Scarborough waterpark is being run by the council while the sale of the attraction to a new owner is completed.

Alpamare, overlooking Scarborough's North Bay, was taken over from Flamingo Land by North Yorkshire Council on 1 November.

The council announced a preferred bidder had been identified in September following a "competitive marketing process", with the authority maintaining the facility "in an operational condition" until it is formally handed over.

The water park is expected to be reopened by the buyer in the first quarter of 2027, according to the council.

The attraction opened in 2016 with the help of a £9m loan from the former Scarborough Borough Council, but its original developer, Benchmark Leisure Ltd, entered administration in 2023.

The authority was left to take possession of the site and write off most of the loan, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

The waterpark reopened in 2024 after local theme park Flamingo Land agreed to operate the facility under lease arrangements from the council, with the agreement expiring at the end of October.

The identity of the preferred buyer has not yet been made public, with further details set to be released once contracts are exchanged and the sale completed.

Councillor Peter Wilkinson, the council's executive member for finance and resources, said: "The council has put arrangements in place to maintain the site in an operational condition during this interim period and facilitate a smooth handover to the purchaser."

articles.title: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page reveals 'awful' comments from male actor
articles.summary: Page spoke of the comments during Tuesday's episode of I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!
articles.body:
Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.

The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.

"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.

Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.

Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".

"And it was just, like, really inappropriate, awful stuff."

Frostrup suggested that if she did speak up people would say she could not "take it", and would call it "banter".

Page then asked her campmates if they thought "we've changed".

"I think it has changed," Frostrup said, "because I look at my daughter now, and she just wouldn't put up with anything like that."

Page, who started out as an actress in 1999, previously revealed in an autobiography that she was warned about a TV presenter being "very handsy" and was groped but stayed silent because she did not want to "make a fuss".

She said she tried to keep it "light-hearted" and "would not have dreamed of making a complaint".

articles.title: An Indiana father living on disability payments was ordered to sell his $270,000 home and help pay for his daughter's college; on November 17, appeals judges kept the sale order but overturned the college costs
articles.summary: An Indiana man who receives disability payments and says he cannot afford to relocate has been ordered to sell his $270,000 marital home as part of his
articles.body: An Indiana man who receives disability payments and says he cannot afford to relocate has been ordered to sell his $270,000 marital home as part of his divorce settlement. However, an appeals court has overturned the order requiring him to contribute towards his daughter's college expenses, citing concerns over his ability to pay.The Indiana Court of Appeals, in a November 17 decision, upheld the trial court's division of marital property, including the sale of the house in Plainfield. But it reversed the direction that the father and his former wife each pay one-third of their daughter's college costs for four years, provided she maintained a cumulative grade point average of at least 2.5.The appeals court said the trial court had not adequately considered the father's financial circumstances or the statutory factors governing orders for post-secondary education expenses.Why the father was asked to sell his $270,000 homeAccording to the court decision, the couple purchased the Plainfield property in 2018 for $172,500. The father continued living there after their separation, while the mother moved out in December 2022. The trial court valued the house at $270,000 and ordered its sale, with the father receiving the first $9,375 from the proceeds as credit for mortgage payments made during the divorce proceedings. The remaining net proceeds were to be divided equally.The father argued that selling the house would cause him hardship. He said he had been unable to work since 2019 and depended entirely on long-term disability payments linked to his previous employment with Amazon. Court records showed that he received about $997 twice a month, or nearly $23,920 annually.He also said he had only $600 in his checking account and could not afford to move or find another place to live. However, the appeals court found no basis to overturn the trial court's division of marital property, noting that the house represented a substantial part of the couple's marital estate.Why the appeals court overturned the college expense orderThe father also challenged the direction to contribute towards his daughter's college education, arguing that the court had failed to account for his limited income and financial obligations.The mother had submitted an estimate showing that attending Indiana University-Indianapolis would cost about $28,430 a year, with grants expected to cover $16,895. The father said he could not afford the additional expense.The appeals court noted that Indiana law requires courts to consider a child's ability to contribute through work, loans or financial aid, as well as each parent's ability to meet the costs. It also said an award should not be made if it would impose a substantial financial burden.Finding that the trial court had not made the required findings, the appeals court reversed the college expense order. It also directed the lower court to divide the costs of the daughter's optional activities according to the parents' incomes, with the father paying 43 per cent and the mother 57 per cent. The court further ruled that the mother should be entitled to claim the children as dependents for tax purposes.The case was sent back to the trial court for an amended divorce decree.You use AI every day. articles.title: Visitors encouraged to 'discover somewhere new' in Yorkshire
articles.summary: An initiative is being launched to try to increase European visitors' interest in Yorkshire.
articles.body:
A new initiative aims to help tourism businesses across Yorkshire attract more visitors to "discover somewhere new" by turning short breaks into longer stays.

A government grant will be used to try to encourage tourists from Europe to visit parts of the area away from the more traditional attractions, said Visit Hull and East Yorkshire (VHEY), which is leading the campaign.

Money will be used to help smaller tourism businesses "prepare their experiences for sale through tour operators".

The project is being supported by all four elected mayors in Yorkshire.

Chris Blacksell, chairman of VHEY, said he hoped the partnership could bring lasting benefits to the region.

"Visitors do not necessarily plan their holidays around destination boundaries," he said.

"They look for experiences that interest them and places they want to explore. By making those connections easier, we can give them more reasons to extend their stay and discover somewhere new."

VHEY said visitor spending in Hull and East Yorkshire reached more than £1bn for the first time in 2024.

However, a recent report said the number of visitors to York between January and June fell by 8% from the same period last year.

Jackie Dad, deputy leader of Hull City Council and vice-chairwoman of VHEY, said the scheme offered an "opportunity to introduce the city to more people as part of a wider Yorkshire experience".

She added: "Connecting our cultural attractions and heritage with other destinations can encourage visitors to include Hull in their plans and spend more time here."

The £160,000 grant comes from the government's Connected Destinations Fund.

VisitEngland chief executive Patricia Yates said: "By encouraging visitors to stay longer and travel further, they will help drive regional growth, support local businesses and spread the economic benefits of tourism more widely."

articles.title: A couple who met at Atlanta's Morris Brown College more than 50 years ago has donated $700,000 to restore an 1882 landmark that has stood unused since 2004, bringing a long-promised $1 million gift closer
articles.summary: Some love stories begin in classrooms, but for Eleanor Powell Clark and Benny Franklin Clark, their connection to Morris Brown College has grown into a
articles.body: Some love stories begin in classrooms, but for Eleanor Powell Clark and Benny Franklin Clark, their connection to Morris Brown College has grown into a lifelong commitment to giving back. More than five decades after meeting at the Atlanta institution, the couple is helping preserve one of its most significant landmarks through a generous financial contribution. Their $700,000 donation towards restoring Fountain Hall brings their long-standing $1 million pledge closer to completion and offers fresh hope for the historic building's revival. The contribution comes at an important time for the historically Black college, which has been working to rebuild its institutional standing and restore its historic campus.Alumni turn gratitude into a major contributionAccording to uATL, the Clarks, both graduates of Morris Brown College, announced their $700,000 donation to support the restoration of Fountain Hall. The contribution forms part of a $1 million commitment that the couple now expects to fulfil earlier than originally anticipated. Their generosity is also intended to encourage other former students to contribute towards preserving the institution's legacy.The Quintessential Gentleman reported that the donation was initially acknowledged without revealing the contributors' identities. College president Dr Kevin James later identified Benny and Eleanor Clark as the benefactors and indicated that additional funds would follow, taking their overall contribution to $1 million. The announcement has brought renewed attention to a restoration project that holds considerable historical and cultural importance for the college.Fountain Hall: A historic landmarkAccording to the official data, the main building of Atlanta University was Fountain Hall, originally Stone Hall, built in 1882. Its association with scholar and civil rights activist W.E.B. Du Bois makes it architecturally and historically significant.According to The Quintessential Gentleman, Du Bois maintained his office in the building between 1897 and 1910 while teaching at Atlanta University. Designed by architect Gottfried L. Norrman in the High Victorian Gothic style, the structure represents an important chapter in the educational history of Atlanta.Following the reorganisation of Atlanta University in 1929, the property was transferred to Morris Brown College. It was subsequently renamed Fountain Hall in honour of Bishop William A. Fountain of the African Methodist Episcopal Church. Its historical importance was formally recognised in 1974 when it received National Historic Landmark designation.The $30 million restoration challenge after decades of decayAlthough historic, Fountain Hall has been neglected and deteriorated for years. The building has remained unused since 2004, while the scale of repairs required has made restoration a considerable financial undertaking.The Quintessential Gentleman reported that the structure was included on the Georgia Trust for Historic Preservation's Places in Peril list in 2019. Morris Brown has estimated that completing the restoration could cost approximately $30 million.The proposed work includes repairing the building's stained-glass windows, installing a new roof and restoring its clock and bell. These initial improvements are important steps towards bringing the landmark back into use.The college has also received support from the National Park Service through a restoration grant, reflecting the wider significance of preserving the historic property.A donation arriving during a college revivalThe Clarks' contribution comes as Morris Brown marks its 145th year and continues its efforts to strengthen its academic future.The institution lost its accreditation in 2002, threatening its future. President Kevin James re-accredited it in 2022. Its student population rose from 20 to around 600. For uATL and The Quintessential Gentleman, Fountain Hall's restoration is essential to the college's comeback and identity.The Clarks see the donation as more than money. “It’s a chance to give back to the institution that educated and united them.” Their contribution could also inspire a wider alumni effort to ensure that Fountain Hall's historic legacy continues for generations to come.Images Courtesy: Discover Atlanta and The Quintessential GentlemanYou use AI every day. articles.title: Microsoft’s massive outage offers a lesson in how to bring the world back online
articles.summary: Microsoft 365's Thursday, Nov. 12 outage had a fix within hours, but the hard part was the restart, as servers brought back too soon collapsed again.
articles.body: When Microsoft 365 went down on Thursday, Nov. 12, the public explanation arrived in pieces: "elevated load," then servers "unexpectedly unavailable," then an overwhelmed process for "establishing secure connections." Each update was accurate. None of them, on its own, told the story. Charles Lamanna, an executive vice president at Microsoft, has since shared a summary of what his teams saw from the inside. It describes one of the hardest problems in large-scale computing: not breaking, but coming back. A bad week for the systems we can’t see DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' Microsoft’s outage turned out to be the start of a bad week. On Friday, Nov. 12, the FAA halted departures nationwide. That evening, Workday, the payroll platform for more than 11,500 organizations, went down after a backup test went wrong. On Monday, Nov. 16, a software bug at JPMorgan Chase slowed transactions, and customers at other banks felt it too. The week wasn’t over. On Tuesday, Nov. 17, the National Security Agency’s classified internal network, NSA Net, suffered an intermittent outage. Sources said there was no sign of a cyberattack and that critical communications stayed intact, and the agency staggered employee arrival times so tens of thousands of people wouldn’t all try to log in at once. Around midday, Apple confirmed problems with iCloud sign-in, the App Store and Apple Music, and users reported Apple Pay trouble too. Thousands of Gmail users reported that messages weren’t arriving, though Google said it saw no evidence of a broad disruption. DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP Different organizations, different causes, no sign they were connected. But together they made one point: how an organization recovers matters as much as why it failed. Microsoft’s recovery is a model of getting that part right. What happened at Microsoft Start with what didn’t happen. No email was lost, and it wasn’t an attack. What did happen was a cascading failure inside Exchange Online, the service behind Microsoft 365 email. At its worst, roughly 80% of the affected servers were unhealthy. And here is the part most people missed: engineers had a fix before service came back. The hardest work was the restart. A cascade works like this. When one server fails, its users don’t disappear. Their mail apps reconnect, and the load lands on the neighbors. If those neighbors were already near their limits, they tip over too. Lamanna described it plainly: one server fell, its load moved to a second, which fell, then a third. Each reconnection also demands a costly encrypted "handshake," so the survivors spent their strength letting people in instead of delivering mail. The strain wasn’t caused by more traffic. The same worldwide demand was simply squeezed onto fewer and fewer healthy machines. The demand never changed. The number of machines left to carry it did. The restart problem So why didn’t service come straight back once engineers had a fix? Utility crews could tell you. After a long blackout, every furnace and refrigerator on a circuit tries to start at once, and the surge can trip the line again. So, crews restore power section by section. They call it cold load pickup. Microsoft faced the digital version. As Lamanna put it, bring back only 20% of the servers, and they go right back down, because the whole world is trying to reach them. Thursday proved it: servers returned that afternoon failed again once evening traffic found them. Thursday night, it looked as though nothing was happening. In fact, the most delicate work of the incident was underway. Engineers took one region at a time, held it fully offline, then brought it from zero to 100% in a single step, so full capacity was ready before full demand arrived. Japan came first, then Europe, the United States and the rest of the world, roughly following the business day around the globe. By Friday morning, email queues were nearly back to normal. What went right Outages at this scale are rare. Responses this disciplined are rarer. Within about three hours, Microsoft froze all deployments and configuration changes so no one could make things worse. It tested its fix on a few servers before rolling it out, and it kept revising its public explanation as the evidence changed instead of defending a first guess. The most important result never made a headline. Email that couldn’t be delivered Thursday waited in queues and arrived Friday. Not a single message was lost. That is the payoff of design decisions made years before anyone needed them. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The lesson isn’t that the cloud is fragile. It’s that at a planetary scale, problems don’t stay small and recovery can’t be rushed. The engineers in Redmond respected that. They resisted the urge to flip every switch at once and brought the world back one region at a time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That isn’t luck. That’s engineering.

articles.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case: What to expect
articles.summary: The ICJ rules on The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar. Here’s what’s at stake for the Rohingya.
articles.body:
On Thursday, November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague will deliver its verdict in a landmark case brought by The Gambia, accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya ethnic minority.

The ruling, which will be final and cannot be appealed, comes seven years after The Gambia filed its case with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and more than nine years after a military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine State forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.

The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim ethnic minority who have lived for centuries in Rakhine State, western Myanmar.

Successive governments, from military rule under General Ne Win (1962 to 1988), to the civilian-led administration of Aung San Suu Kyi (2016 to 2021), have consistently treated them as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh, while a 1982 citizenship law left most of them stateless.

They have faced repeated waves of violence and displacement, but the crisis came to a head in August 2017.

When fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) – a rebel group – attacked police posts, the military launched what it called “clearance operations” across northern Rakhine.

Survivors described massacres, rapes and entire villages burned to the ground, and more than 740,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh within months.

In November 2019, The Gambia took Myanmar to the ICJ, arguing that it had breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.

At the time, Myanmar was led by Aung San Suu Kyi’s civilian government, but the military, under commander-in-chief Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, controlled the security forces which carried out the crackdown.

Min Aung Hlaing’s military government then came to power in a 2021 coup and has defended the case at the ICJ.

Myanmar denies the charge, saying its forces were responding to armed attacks.

Unlike in a criminal trial, the ICJ does not judge individuals. It asks whether Myanmar as a state is responsible for genocide, and what it must do to make amends.

Today, about 520,000 Rohingya remain in Myanmar, many living under severe restrictions, while about 1.2 million are refugees in Bangladesh.

They are widely dispersed, with most still unable to return to their homes.

Nearly nine years after the 2017 exodus, about 1.2 million Rohingya are still living in Bangladesh, mostly in the crowded refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar.

Bangladesh, which wants them to return to Myanmar, restricts their movement and limits their access to formal work, leaving families heavily dependent on aid .

That aid has been severely curtailed over the years.

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of deepening insecurity and fewer long-term solutions, made worse by cuts to life-saving aid.

Shortly after US President Donald Trump commenced his second term in the White House in 2025, his administration froze or cut much of the country’s foreign aid, disrupting aid programmes in Bangladesh. Other countries have also cut foreign aid spending as costs elsewhere have risen in recent years.

A UNHCR study found that these cuts have weakened services for refugees such as registration, legal aid, healthcare, education and child protection, exposing refugees to greater risks of trafficking, forced labour and child marriage.

For the roughly 520,000 Rohingya still in Myanmar since the 2017 crackdown, conditions have worsened since the country’s 2021 military coup.

The Arakan Army, a rebel group fighting for autonomy for Rakhine, now controls most of Rakhine State. It has been accused of seizing land, arbitrary killings and torture, while the military has forcibly conscripted Rohingya men to fight against it.

In August 2024, hundreds of Rohingya fleeing fighting in Maungdaw were reportedly killed by drone and artillery strikes while crossing the Naf River into Bangladesh.

Su Mon, Asia Pacific senior analyst at ACLED , said: “These conditions prevent any safe, voluntary, or dignified return of Rohingya refugees. All communities in Rakhine State face severe food insecurity, lack of aid, an economic collapse, and relentless conflict.”

With little hope at home or in the camps, thousands have been boarding boats to Malaysia and Indonesia each year.

The UNHCR estimates 3,135 people have died or gone missing at sea since 2022, while 2025 was the deadliest year on record, with 900 lives lost.

What is The Gambia arguing, and how has Myanmar responded?

The Gambia , a small Muslim-majority country in West Africa, has no direct connection to the violence in Myanmar. It brought the case on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), of which it is an active member.

Some observers also link The Gambia’s position to its own history. As the Rohingya crisis unfolded, the country was investigating killings and abductions committed under former leader Yahya Jammeh, who ruled for 22 years until 2017.

The Gambia accuses Myanmar’s military of killing Rohingya, causing physical and mental harm, imposing conditions designed to destroy the group and preventing births during its so-called “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine.

It also described widespread sexual violence, which it alleges is a central part of this campaign.

Myanmar says its operations targeted Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) fighters and their supporters, accusing The Gambia of downplaying the threat they posed.

The key question the court has examined is whether Myanmar intended to destroy the Rohingya as a group, a requirement for proving genocide.

The Gambia points to the brutality of the attacks, official tolerance of hate speech and the failure to investigate abuses as evidence of that intent.

Myanmar says there is no direct evidence of such intent and that The Gambia has failed to prove it.

The Gambia is asking the court to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible and to ensure the Rohingya can safely return home. Other demands include restoring their property, recognising their right to identify as Rohingya and providing compensation where property cannot be returned.

Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on behalf of Rohingya victims.

What happens if Myanmar is found guilty of genocide?

The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed, and Myanmar is legally bound to follow it. But the ICJ has no way to enforce its decisions.

If Myanmar ignores the ruling, The Gambia can ask the UN Security Council to act. The council has never used this power and any of its five permanent members could block action with a veto. China and Russia have shielded Myanmar there before.

Other countries and the UN General Assembly can also apply political pressure on Myanmar to comply.

The court could also stop short of a genocide finding. In 2007, it ruled that Serbia had not committed genocide in Bosnia, but had failed to prevent the Srebrenica massacre .

How often has the ICJ issued a genocide verdict?

The ICJ has rarely found a state responsible for genocide, largely because proving intent to destroy a group is very difficult.

In 2007, the court ruled that Serbia was not directly responsible for committing genocide in Bosnia. However, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed.

How judges apply this high legal threshold in the Myanmar case will be closely watched, particularly for what it could mean for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over Gaza.

Currently, there are four other genocide cases before the court:

Ukraine v Russia, filed in February 2022 – Pending.

South Africa v Israel, filed in December 2023 over Israel’s war on Gaza – Pending.

Nicaragua v Germany, filed in March 2024 over Germany’s support for Israel – Awaiting a ruling on jurisdiction.

Democratic Republic of the Congo v Rwanda, filed in June 2026 – Pending.

articles.title: US Democrats probe whether Lutnick used office to protect sons' firm amid Nvidia controversy
articles.summary: US Democratic lawmakers have opened an investigation into commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.
articles.body: US Democratic lawmakers have opened an investigation into commerce secretary Howard Lutnick. They are examining whether he used his government position to protect Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm now controlled by his sons, from potential financial losses linked to a controversy surrounding Nvidia, the Financial Times reported.In a letter to Cantor Fitzgerald chair Brandon Lutnick, the commerce secretary's 28-year-old son, three Democratic lawmakers sought information on whether decisions taken by his father were influenced by the firm's investments, business relationships or financial exposure.The inquiry follows an FT report that the Commerce Department delayed efforts to place Megaspeed, a company linked to an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, on the US government's entity list. The list identifies companies Washington considers a national security risk and restricts their access to American technology.US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over suspicions that it smuggled advanced chips to China. The government confirmed on Monday that a criminal investigation was ongoing. Megaspeed has denied the allegations.The lawmakers – Jamie Raskin, Gregory Meeks and Sydney Kamlager-Dove – questioned whether Cantor's financial interests influenced Lutnick's handling of the case, including his reported opposition to adding Megaspeed to the entity list or requiring a licence for exports of advanced AI chips to the company.“Did concerns about your company’s financial exposure, business relationships, or contractual and commitments to foreign governments influence secretary Lutnick’s refusal to add Megaspeed to the entity list or to require a licence for the export of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed?” they asked in the letter, seen by the FT.Cantor denies having material Nvidia exposureThe controversy also centres on Cantor Fitzgerald's reported holdings in Nvidia and its business with data centre operators in Southeast Asia. The New York Times has reported that some of these operators provide AI computing capacity to Chinese groups.Regulatory filings compiled by Bloomberg show Cantor reported holding about one million Nvidia shares at the end of the third quarter, worth roughly $155 million at current prices. That was down from three million shares at the end of last year.Cantor said the allegations in the lawmakers' letter were “inaccurate” and insisted it had “no material proprietary position in Nvidia”. It said its reported holdings reflected shares bought to hedge trades for clients, and that the decline resulted from customers changing their trading positions rather than a decision by the firm.The company also said it had no role in US export-control or entity-list decisions. Its work with Southeast Asian data centre operators, it said, was part of its “ordinary-course investment banking business”.“Allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless,” Cantor said.Lutnick's business interests under scrutinyAfter taking charge of the Commerce Department last year, Lutnick transferred control of his Wall Street brokerage to trusts benefiting his sons, Brandon and Kyle. The department said on Tuesday that he had divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, as well as in property group Newmark and brokerage BGC.The Commerce Department said Lutnick makes policy decisions in the best interests of the United States and had fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including requirements on divestment and recusal.The Democratic lawmakers have asked Brandon Lutnick to preserve all potentially relevant records linked to the inquiry. Raskin is the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, while Meeks holds the same position on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.Both committees are currently led by Republicans, but Democrats are set to take control of the House in January following their victory in this month's midterm elections. The shift is likely to give the party greater scope to investigate the Trump administration.Raskin recently told the FT that Democrats were identifying their priorities for investigations next year amid what he described as an “avalanche of corruption” in the Trump administration.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
articles.summary: The three leaders will meet together for the first time on Thursday during a closely-watched summit.
articles.body:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.

After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.

Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.

However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Trump have not yet held a substantive meeting, and merely greeted each other on Wednesday.

Peskov also said that "no more than an hour" had been allocated for Thursday's trilateral talks between Putin, Trump and Xi.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.

It is unclear whether China would want this issue to be on the agenda in Shenzhen, with Beijing talking more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.

Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.

Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".

In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.

Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".

Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.

The south-east Chinese city the Apec summit is being held in is a booming area for manufacturing and advanced tech.

It comes against the backdrop of the ousting of Nvidia chief executing Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of spying for Beijing - a claim dismissed as a "smear" by China.

Trump has pursued warmer relations with China but the incident points to ongoing tensions between the two powers.

Several hours before Trump's arrival, Putin landed in Shenzhen and held around two hours of talks with Xi, with whom he has pressed for closer economic and defence relations.

Xi said both countries would "move forward steadily and boldly" and that the relationship was "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".

articles.title: 'A lot of it is connected': Rahul Gandhi links India, France, US to global economic shifts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday linked democratic challenges across countries, including India to broader changes in the global
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday linked democratic challenges across countries, including India to broader changes in the global economy, saying "a lot of it is connected".Speaking at a fireside chat at Columbia University, Rahul Gandhi was asked whether democracy and diversity in India had been undervalued during the Narendra Modi government's tenure, with the question referring to the centralisation of power and the treatment of different social groups.In response, the Lok Sabha leader of opposition said similar trends were visible across several countries and argued that they were connected to broader changes in the global economic structure.“Well, the interesting question is, why is that happening in so many places in the world? Why is it happening in one way in the United States? Why is it happening in Brazil? Why is it happening in so many different places? So it can't be that all these countries are coming to the same conclusion at the same time without there being some connection between them. So to me, you can't separate what is happening in India or what is happening in France with what is happening on the planet with what is happening to the larger substrate, larger economic substrate. And to me, a lot of it is connected,” Rahul said.He cited the inability of several countries to create enough jobs for blue-collar workers, contrasting their struggles with China's manufacturing and employment record.“So, for example, how does India give its blue collar workers a job? How does America give its blue collar workers a job? How does France give its blue collar workers a job? None of them seem to be able to do it. Right. So there is something that has happened at a global level where China has no problem giving its blue collar labor a job. Right? But somehow everybody else seems to be struggling with it. So that, to me is a interesting question,” he added.Earlier during the interaction, he also described India's economy as an “economic disaster”, citing unemployment, problems in the education system and a struggling manufacturing sector.He said the country's economic model had stopped delivering results almost a decade ago and criticised government initiatives such as Make in India and Startup India, PTI reported.“The blunt thing is that India is sitting on an economic disaster. That's the reality of it. One can brush it aside; the media can brush it aside. But India has got a massive unemployment problem. India's got a massive problem with its education system,” he said.“The spine of the economy is small and medium businesses, which are the job creation engine, and agriculture. That is fundamental in India and required,” he said, adding that the “spine of the economy has been broken,” he added.He also questioned the lack of private investment and alleged that only a few large business groups, including those led by Gautam Adani and Mukesh Ambani, were expanding while smaller businesses struggled."We cannot survive successfully without manufacturing; it just cannot be done," he added.BJP hit back at Rahul over his remarks, with party president Nitin Nabin alleging that the “disaster” lay in the Congress leader's own mind and accusing him of overlooking India's economic progress.Speaking to reporters, Nabin said major institutions had acknowledged improvements in people's development and a rise in per capita income."I suspect that the 'disaster' actually resides within his own mind, perhaps because his family, his party, and he himself have failed to grow, he chooses to label the economy a 'disaster.' Major institutions acknowledge that the development of India's people has progressed, and per capita income has risen; yet, he fails to see this development," Nabin said."Rahul Gandhi describes India's economy as a 'disaster.' He has raised questions about all of the country's constitutional institutions—ironic, coming from those who frequently invoke democracy, yet have been responsible for its greatest subversions. I would like to ask Rahul Gandhi: global financial institutions—such as the World Bank, the IMF, and others—recognise India's growth, acknowledging that, despite global instability, India is the fastest-growing nation. We are currently growing at a rate of 7.1%, in line with international standards," he added.BJP national general secretary Tarun Chugh also criticised Rahul, claiming that while world leaders and international agencies recognised India as a “global growth engine”, the Congress leader viewed the country through an “Italian lens”.Rahul is on a two-day visit to the United States. He is scheduled to visit the University of Chicago on Wednesday.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Medicare premiums are rising in 2027. What you'll pay and how much of your Social Security raise you'll keep.
articles.summary: Here's what charges are in store for Medicare Part A, Part B and Part D, and how much of the $75 average COLA increase you'll keep.
articles.body:
Medicare Part B premiums will rise by 3.2% in 2027, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced Tuesday .

The standard premium will rise by $6.50 per month to $209.40, totaling a $78-per-year increase.

The 2027 increase, far smaller than the nearly 10% increase enrollees faced in 2026, is in line with the 3.25% increase projected by Medicare's trustees.

According to the CMS, "The increase in the 2027 Part B standard premium and deductible is mainly due to projected increases in healthcare spending."

Here's what you need to know before the increases are applied in January.

The Medicare Part A deductible, which beneficiaries pay if they are admitted to the hospital, will rise by $40 to $1,776 in 2027.

The Medicare Part A premium will be $597 per month, a $32 increase from $565 in 2026.

Anyone aged 65 and older with fewer than 40 quarters of coverage, plus certain people with disabilities.

Uninsured people aged 65 and older with fewer than 30 quarters, and certain people with disabilities who have exhausted other entitlements.

Those with at least 30 quarters (or a spouse with 30 or more quarters) will pay a reduced rate of $328.

Roughly 9% of people with Part B pay an income-related surcharge on top of their monthly premium.

The annual deductible for all Medicare Part B beneficiaries will increase by $9 to $292 in 2027.

In 2027, individuals with modified adjusted gross income above $112,000, or couples filing jointly above $224,000, will pay more. At the top tier, individuals with an income of $500,000 or more and couples earning $750,000 or more will pay $711.80 a month.

Married people who live with their spouse but file separate tax returns pay the standard $209.40 Part B premium if their income is $112,000 or less. Above that, they pay a total of $670 a month, rising to $711.80 for those earning $388,000 or more.

A small group of kidney transplant patients can keep Part B coverage of immunosuppressive drugs for a standard premium of $125.70 a month.

Those with higher incomes who pay Part D premiums face separate income-related surcharges between $15.40 and $96.40 a month on top of their plan's premium. The surcharge is paid to Medicare and is either deducted from Social Security checks or paid directly.

People who have their Part B premium deducted from their Social Security checks will keep less of the cost-of-living adjustment next year.

For the average retiree, the $6.50 Part B increase will eat into the $75 monthly COLA boost, leaving them with about $68.50 more a month.

Most beneficiaries will have the standard $209.40 Part B premium withheld from their checks. Higher earners will pay more, with total monthly Part B premiums reaching as much as $711.80 and Part D surcharges up to $96.40.

articles.title: William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi
articles.summary: The meeting in New Delhi was a late addition to the royal couple's India visit, which has also included their appearance at the annual Earthshot Prize
articles.body:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have reflected on the enduring ties between the UK and India with its Prime Minister Narendra Modi, as they wrapped up their three-day visit to India.

William and Catherine arrived in New Delhi on Wednesday for the final leg of their first official overseas trip together in four years.

The meeting was a late addition to the couple's schedule and came after Modi confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.

It comes a day after the royal couple were in Mumbai for the annual Earthshot Prize, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.

Street cricket with a legend then metro ride as William and Kate begin India visit

A Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".

The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and added how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.

Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the India-UK partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".

The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.

When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.

The royak spokesperson said that the meeting touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".

The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

William and Catherine's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.

As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.

And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.

articles.title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
articles.summary: Bahrain says it was also attacked by Iran following a US air strike on the Iranian island of Qeshm in the Gulf on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.

The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.

It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.

The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.

The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.

Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump

Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington

Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.

The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".

"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.

Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".

The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.

Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".

The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.

Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.

"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.

On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.

Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.

Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".

At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

articles.title: Police investigate death of boy, 3, after nursery incident
articles.summary: The boy died in hospital three days after an incident at Cosy Toes Nursery in Middleton, police say.
articles.body:
An investigation has been launched into the death of a three-year-old boy following an incident at a nursery in Greater Manchester, police said.

The boy became critically ill at Cosy Toes Nursery in Middleton shortly before 16:00 GMT on Monday 2 November.

He was rushed to hospital, where he died three days later.

Greater Manchester Police said his family were being supported by specialist officers.

Det Ch Insp Claire Brennan said: "This is an incredibly tragic development in a deeply upsetting incident and our thoughts remain with the boy's family."

Police said an investigation had been launched in line with standard procedure following a child's death in a care setting.

A spokeswoman for Cosy Toes said they were "all heartbroken" by the "wonderful and beautiful" boy's death.

"Our thoughts and prayers are all with his family at this terrible time," she said.

"We will of course give our fullest possible assistance in every way possible to the enquiries that must rightly follow this tragic event."

Anyone with information about the boy's death is being urged to contact police.

Brennan said: "We are in the very early stages of our involvement and are carefully considering events and the evidence available to us.

"For now, we ask that the family's privacy is respected as they begin to navigate the unimaginable loss of their little boy."

Ofsted said it had taken the decision to suspend the nursery's registration in the wake of the incident, meaning the nursery will be closed for six weeks as investigations are carried out.

A spokesperson said: "Our thoughts are with the family of the young boy and everyone affected by this deeply distressing and tragic incident.

"We have worked closely with the police, and we have suspended the nursery's registration. We will continue to support the police and other agencies in their enquiries. We are unable to comment further while the police investigation is ongoing."
