articles.title: Beyond Nvidia scandal: The psychology of honey traps and vulnerabilities they exploit
articles.summary: A beautiful stranger, a chance encounter, a seemingly genuine romance and eventually, a request that could compromise national security.
articles.body: A beautiful stranger, a chance encounter, a seemingly genuine romance and eventually, a request that could compromise national security.It sounds like a plot straight out of a James Bond film, where seduction is as potent a weapon as a gun or a spy gadget. But in the real world, the art of turning intimacy into intelligence is far from fiction.From the Soviet KGB's female operatives and East Germany's Romeo spies during the Cold War to alleged Chinese intelligence links surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, honey trapping has remained a potent tool in the world of espionage.The methods may have evolved, but the underlying strategy remains remarkably unchanged: exploit human relationships to gain access to information, influence or leverage that conventional intelligence-gathering methods may struggle to obtain.The latest controversy involving Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang and Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, has brought renewed attention to the use of personal relationships in espionage.According to reports by The New York Times, Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based data-centre company Megaspeed International.Huang later acknowledged having an extramarital affair in an apology to his family and Nvidia employees, but did not name the woman.US intelligence officials reportedly suspect Alice Huang of passing information to the Chinese government and have examined her alleged links to China's ministry of state security (MSS), its civilian intelligence agency.However, it remains unclear whether she was recruited by Chinese intelligence, what information she may have obtained, or whether any sensitive information was shared.Beijing has dismissed the allegations as "groundless speculation".The case has raised concerns about how personal relationships could potentially be exploited to gain access to influential corporate leaders and sensitive information, particularly amid growing US-China rivalry over artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology.It has also brought the spotlight back on honey trapping, an age-old espionage that continues to find relevance in the digital age.From KGB 'swallows' to Romeo spiesHoney trapping is hardly a new invention. During the Cold War, the Soviet KGB deployed female agents, commonly associated with the terms 'sparrows' or 'swallows', to cultivate relationships with Western diplomats and officials.Male operatives were also used, while East Germany's Stasi became particularly notorious for its so-called Romeo spies.The objective was to establish intimacy and trust, obtain sensitive information or create compromising situations that could later be exploited through blackmail.One of the best-known examples involved East German spymaster Markus Wolf's Romeo operations. Male agents were sent to West Germany to cultivate relationships with women working as secretaries in sensitive government offices.One of the best-known examples involved an East German operative codenamed Felix, who recruited Norma, a West German government employee.She went on to pass him confidential information from the West German chancellery. According to the CIA, 40 women were prosecuted in West Germany for espionage during the Cold War.The Soviet KGB also used sexual blackmail to recruit John Vassall, an employee at the British embassy in Moscow. He was photographed in compromising circumstances and threatened with exposure. Fearing that his private life would be revealed, Vassall eventually passed documents to Soviet intelligence.The tactic was not limited to heterosexual relationships or female operatives. In a famous case that later inspired the play and film M. Butterfly, French diplomat Bernard Boursicot had a nearly two-decade relationship with Chinese opera singer Shi Pei Pu, who concealed his gender.Boursicot, then a 20-year-old embassy clerk, met Shi at a Christmas party in Beijing in 1964. Shi, a performer with the Beijing Opera who also taught Chinese to diplomats' families, told him he was a woman forced to live as a man.Boursicot believed the claim, and the friendship developed into a romantic relationship. Shi later claimed to have given birth to their child, further reinforcing Boursicot's belief.The relationship took an espionage turn when Chinese security officials reportedly discovered the affair. Chinese intelligence eventually used the relationship to pressure Boursicot into handing over information from the French embassy.Boursicot said he had believed Shi was a woman throughout their relationship; the revelation became one of the most striking elements of a case that blurred the lines between romance, deception and espionage.Another case involved Chinese-American Katrina Leung, who was paid by the FBI to provide information on China. However, she was later accused of acting as a double agent and passing classified information to Beijing.She was also romantically involved with two FBI agents, including her longtime handler. Leung and the handler were arrested in 2003.The cases underline how intimacy, emotional attachment and the fear of exposure can become instruments of intelligence gathering.How intelligence agencies identify their targetsThe targets of honey-trap operations are not necessarily politicians or military officers. Anyone with access to sensitive information or the ability to influence important decisions can attract the attention of foreign intelligence agencies.Corporate executives, technology leaders, diplomats, defence personnel and government officials may all be of interest, particularly when their work involves strategic technologies, classified information or policy decisions."There are structural mechanisms within each organisation across the world to identify a person of interest, and mapping their life in general and professional settings. While dossiers support the research, identifying a low hanging fruit or sub set of the POI is where the ground work is laid," sources in the security establishment told TOI."Intelligence agencies constantly seek and look for individuals who have access to information or can influence important decisions, irrespective of corporate executives, diplomats or military personnel. Now more than ever, with social media sites permeating every part of our lives, identifying and mapping individuals makes it easier than ever before," the sources said."Agencies have ample access to play out vulnerabilities of the individual and map an entire operation before it is even launched. Anyone within the map of the Person Of Interest can be used as a bait," they added.The process, therefore, may begin long before a target realises they are being approached. Intelligence agencies can study an individual's professional responsibilities, social circles, interests and personal vulnerabilities before deciding how to cultivate access.From dating apps to AI: How the game has changedThe digital world has significantly expanded the possibilities for intelligence gathering. Social media platforms, dating applications and professional networking sites offer information about people's interests, relationships, movements and professional associations.What once required physical surveillance and prolonged groundwork can now begin with information available online.Artificial intelligence has added another dimension, making it easier to analyse publicly available information and build detailed profiles of potential targets."Social media and dating applications have made it easier than ever before for intelligence agencies to map, draw, profile and act on an individual across the geographical boundaries with or without physical or direct contact or via intermediaries. Any person of interest in any government, military or official capacity is fair game, more often than not without them realising the pitfalls of it,” the sources told TOI."Proliferation of artificial intelligence has made it easy to map the life of an entire individual and their lives even with snippets of publicly available information. Protecting data takes precedence in the age of AI on steroids," they added.Modern honey traps do not always begin with a trained agent approaching a target with the intention of seducing them.In some cases, an individual may develop a relationship organically with someone of interest to an intelligence agency. The agency may subsequently identify the opportunity and recruit that person, through incentives or coercion, to obtain information.Former CIA intelligence officer John Sipher has pointed out that authoritarian governments may have greater latitude to use pressure and manipulation when recruiting individuals."What the Chinese and Russians and others can do is, they can use much more manipulation and pressure (to recruit a spy)," Sipher told CNN, adding that "They can say, 'Listen, we won't let you return home, or you won't be able to see your family, unless you work with us.'"Another method involves placing an individual in a compromising situation and subsequently using the threat of exposure or arrest to extract cooperation.However, the more familiar cinematic version, in which a trained foreign agent deliberately seduces a target from the outset and is reportedly less common than often portrayed.When romance meets cyber espionageThe intersection of personal relationships, digital platforms and intelligence gathering has also come under scrutiny in India recently following an alleged honey-trap operation involving an Indian Air Force Wing Commander.According to a Delhi Police chargesheet, the serving officer allegedly shared sensitive information, including details of India's war plans, with a Pakistan-based intelligence operative.The woman allegedly established contact with the officer through WhatsApp, posing as someone seeking help from a qualified therapist.Investigators suspect she exploited his personal circumstances, including his reported marital separation, to establish an emotional connection.Their conversations allegedly became increasingly personal, eventually leading to an exchange of “nude” photographs.The operative allegedly used the relationship to obtain confidential military information and subsequently attempted to expand access by sending malware.The chargesheet further alleges that the officer was instructed to install the software on the mobile phones and laptops of five subordinate officers, potentially exposing their data and communications.He was arrested on May 30, 2026, and the Delhi Police Special Cell subsequently filed a chargesheet. The case is awaiting cognisance by the court, and the allegations are yet to be established through trial.The case also highlights how personal manipulation can be combined with cyber espionage to gain access to information beyond the original target.Addressing the broader threat, IAF chief Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said honey trapping was only one aspect of a wider espionage challenge. "It is not a honeytrap thing. It is basically a cyber espionage issue," he said.“Nowadays espionage happens through cyber means, various other means and enticing. Honeytrap is only one aspect of the overall picture. Multi-level marketing is there and loan sharks are there. They're also active. So we are fully aware of this. We are keeping a close eye and there is a systemic effort to control this,” he added.He also pointed out that since sensitive military communication networks are air-gapped, foreign intelligence handlers may increasingly seek to exploit human operators to gain access to information.Why even powerful people fall preyProfessional success, intelligence and experience do not necessarily make individuals immune to manipulation.Experts say honey-trap operations exploit vulnerabilities that are fundamentally human, including loneliness, ambition, greed, ego and the desire for emotional validation.According to the security agencies, the effectiveness of such operations lies in understanding human behaviour and exploiting motivations that can make individuals susceptible to recruitment."It all comes down to the psychology of the human mind and how effective low cost structures of intelligence operations can yield the most for the buck. Honey trapping remains effective because technology has evolved whereas human nature remains the same. Identifying target, mapping the overarching societal behaviour and preying on the principal is the key to a successful intelligence operation,” the security agencies sources said.MICE – Money, Ideology, Coercion and Ego – explains four traditional motivations exploited in intelligence recruitment and selection of prey for Honey trap is the linchpin of such an operation. No amount of safeguards or technological advancement can beat the old fashioned way of HUMINT.The MICE framework is commonly used in intelligence circles to explain why individuals may be recruited or compromised. Money, ideological beliefs, coercion and ego can all be exploited to establish influence over a target.The vulnerability is not necessarily limited to romantic relationships. Professional friendships, financial arrangements and other personal associations can also become channels through which information is obtained.How to recognise the warning signsWhile no individual can entirely eliminate the possibility of being targeted, experts say awareness and early reporting are important safeguards. Sources said that professional experience does not necessarily translate into personal security awareness."Humans greed of all and any kind is the key answer to why individuals fall prey, despite warnings, awareness, and understanding or the lack thereof. Professional experience does not guarantee personal security awareness. Anyone and everyone can be manipulated, irrespective of their moral compass,” the security agencies sources told TOI."There are ample information and dossiers available to identify warning signs including unusually rapid emotional intimacy, excessive interest in professional responsibilities, demands for secrecy, reluctance to verify identity and requests for sensitive information or intimate photographs,” they said."Sensitive organisations conduct regular counterintelligence awareness programmes covering social engineering, digital impersonation and blackmail. The most important safeguard is early reporting of an iota of suspicious activity and behaviour, irrespective of the situation," the sources added.For organisations, this means strengthening counterintelligence awareness, educating employees about social engineering and digital impersonation, and ensuring that suspicious approaches can be reported without fear of embarrassment or repercussions.Ultimately, the methods of espionage may change, but the human element remains difficult to secure.As the Nvidia controversy and the alleged targeting of Indian defence personnel illustrate, the objective is not always to recruit a conventional spy. Sometimes, all an intelligence agency needs is a relationship that offers access to the right person.As the saying goes in the world of espionage, the most valuable intelligence may not always be behind a firewall. Sometimes, it is just one relationship away.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Another endless war? Saudi Arabia prepares for prolonged fight against Yemen's Houthis
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia is preparing for a conflict with Yemen's Houthi rebels that could continue for up to six months, extending into next year, as the kingdom
articles.body: Saudi Arabia is preparing for a conflict with Yemen's Houthi rebels that could continue for up to six months, extending into next year, as the kingdom seeks to reverse battlefield setbacks and contain attacks on its territory, according to three sources familiar with its plans.Two Western officials briefed by Saudi counterparts said Riyadh expects the campaign to continue for several months, with the aim of securing gains on the ground through its Yemeni allies before entering negotiations with the Houthis. A third source familiar with the plans confirmed their accounts. All three spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations with Saudi officials, Reuters reported.The third source said Saudi Arabia believes that US offensive support for its operations in Yemen, which the administration of President Donald Trump has so far withheld, could alter the course of the conflict and allow Saudi-backed forces to make the desired territorial gains within weeks.The sources also said that an agreement to end the wider war involving Iran could lead to a reduction in fighting in Yemen.The renewed conflict has become the most active front in the wider Iran war, killing and injuring thousands and displacing hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen. It has also disrupted Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract non-oil investment and host major international events.Battlefield setbacks for Saudi-backed forcesSaudi Arabia entered the Yemen conflict in 2015, leading an Arab coalition that sought to restore the country's government to power after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and large parts of the country. The fighting resulted in a bloody stalemate before a ceasefire was reached in 2022. The truce held until the conflict resumed this summer.Since fighting restarted, the Houthis have seized the Red Sea coast and the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait from forces backed by Saudi Arabia. They have also encircled Taiz, a city in the highlands overlooking Aden, the government's temporary capital on Yemen's southern coast.Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive last month and recaptured territory around the strait. However, they withdrew over the past weekend to protect Aden, marking a setback for the Saudi-backed side.Saudi and Yemeni forces are now reorganising to defend Aden against further Houthi advances. They are also considering shifting their offensive towards eastern fronts, where they have made some progress or managed to hold their positions, one of the Western officials said.Saudi Arabia announced on Monday that it had replaced the commander overseeing the Saudi-led coalition. Yemen's government is also expected to reshuffle its military leadership, according to two people familiar with the plans.Saudi Arabia shifts public messaging on warSaudi Arabia had previously sought to portray the renewed conflict as an internal Yemeni issue, with the kingdom supporting its allies in Yemen while defending itself against cross-border attacks, rather than presenting itself as a direct party to the war.However, repeated attacks on Saudi cities have made that position increasingly difficult to maintain. The kingdom has gradually begun acknowledging the conflict and its domestic impact through public statements and messaging in the media and mosques.A Houthi attack last week tore a large hole in the headquarters of state oil company Aramco in Riyadh. A series of deadly strikes on the Saudi capital's airport has also kept it closed to most flights since October.The disruptions have led to the cancellation or postponement of major events, including the flagship Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference. The AFC Asian Cup, a key event in Saudi Arabia's efforts to establish itself as a major destination for international sport, has also been postponed from January 2027 to December of the same year.Since last month, Saudi authorities have been issuing regular alerts ahead of attacks, followed by more detailed statements about the incidents. This marks a shift from their earlier approach of releasing comparatively limited information.Although laws criminalising the distribution of images of attack sites have restricted the circulation of such footage, the deputy governor of Riyadh visited the Aramco Tower two days after it was hit, and state media broadcast images showing the damage.The shift in public messaging has also extended to mosques, where the government guides the themes of sermons that generally focus on everyday issues such as marriage and good neighbourliness.Last Friday, the conflict with the Houthis dominated the sermon at one of Riyadh's larger mosques. The imam promised fighters "victory or martyrdom" and offered prayers for Saudi soldiers stationed along the kingdom's southern border."Oh Allah, guide their aim and steady their feet, and grant them victory over those who show them hostility," he said.Strategic importance of Bab el-Mandeb StraitYemen, a mountainous and largely impoverished country with a heavily armed and tribal society, lies in the south-western corner of the Arabian Peninsula. It has two coastlines, one facing the Indian Ocean and the other the Red Sea.The port city of Aden, once a prosperous trading centre, lies along the Indian Ocean coast. On the Red Sea side is the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow maritime passage at the southern entrance to the waterway. Its name translates into English as the "Gate of Tears".Control of the strait carries significant strategic importance because it allows the holder to threaten maritime traffic travelling between the Mediterranean, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.You use AI every day. articles.title: No Gloucester Cathedral staff to face compulsory redundancy
articles.summary: Gloucester Cathedral has been going through a restructure due to "significant financial pressure".
articles.body:
There will be no compulsory redundancies at a cathedral despite a restructure of staff, leaders have said.

Gloucester Cathedral, which costs about £10,500 a day to open, has been undergoing an organisational restructure due to rising costs as some staff have opted for voluntary redundancies.

It comes after cathedral bosses across the West of England said they had also been feeling the pinch, forcing them to find creative ways to raise money.

Dean of Gloucester Reverend Andrew Zihni said the decision to reshape the cathedral's money was "difficult but necessary" to ensure its future.

Zihni said that visitors to the cathedral are unlikely to notice any changes.

Cathedral chiefs said the restructure involved a review of staff roles and responsibilities, as well as how the organisation is run.

A small number of staff had been made voluntarily redundant as a result of the changes.

In a statement, cathedral leaders said that these had been "very difficult decisions," but that these changes will ensure it will continue to serve the "city, county and wider community for generations to come".

Speaking to BBC Radio Gloucestershire, Zihni said the cathedral had a number of costs, including heating, maintenance and staffing, as well as safeguarding, education, worship, music and heritage.

"We have to raise the money year on year through donations, visitors, grants, fundraising and other income because we don't have any automatic funding either from the national church or the government," he said.

Gloucester Cathedral is not the only one in the country with high maintenance costs.

Anna Pitt, executive director of the Association of English Cathedrals, said it costs more than £30,000 a day to "simply open the doors" at Canterbury Cathedral and York Minster.

"The scale of what cathedrals offer is considerable. They employ 6,000 people across the sector, welcome nearly 10 million visitors each year and are open 365 days a year," said Pitt.

Zihni said the Chapter, who are responsible for running the cathedral, are also looking at ways to "diversify their income stream and develop commercial angles".

He said: "People may have seen some of it already with the concerts we've been hosting in the cathedral, but there isn't a separation between the commercial activity and the regular activity," he said.

articles.title: Georgia built two oyster reefs in the Savannah River in 2023; nearly 18 months later, oyster cover reached 17%–40%, and wave energy was 40% lower than at control sites
articles.summary: Discover how Georgia's oyster reef restoration project in the Savannah River is reducing wave energy by 40%, offering a natural solution to coastal erosion and benefiting marine ecosystems.
articles.body: Oyster reefs are also gaining recognition as a natural solution to guard vulnerable riverbanks from wave damage. To complement conventional engineered coastal defences like anchored concrete barriers or permanently fixed seawalls, these growing oyster populations are acting as a natural buffer to dissipate waves and reduce wave impacts.According to a 2025 study published in Ecological Engineering, oyster reef restoration may be a viable solution to safeguard erosion-vulnerable areas, especially in places with a substantial amount of boat activity. The study measured two restored reefs along Georgia’s Savannah River, where oyster recovery had reached 17% to 40% after almost 18 months. The reefs also blocked up to 40% of the power compared with nearby control sites without reefs.How Georgia constructed the oyster reefsGeorgia deployed the two reefs in May 2023 in the intertidal zone of the Savannah River near Savannah. Researchers identified areas susceptible to erosion, including spots with regularly generated waves and areas with fluctuating water conditions. For the restoration, researchers focused on a technique called spat-on-shell construction. The term spat refers to tiny oysters that attach to a substrate at the beginning of their lives. In this process, prepared oyster shells became a surface for young oysters to attach and grow until a reef forms.Reefs were placed about one to two metres from the marsh edge. They were designed to break incoming waves before the water interacted with the vulnerable marsh plants and exposed sediments. This configuration allowed the structures to serve as living breakwaters while creating ideal conditions for oysters to flourish. The Savannah River was a fitting location to try this technique due to its high boat traffic. Commercial vessels passing by the Port of Savannah and recreational vessels can cause consistent waves to beat against the shoreline, which can lead to the loss of sediments and marsh edge erosion over time.Oyster growth and wave measurements show promising resultsScientists surveyed the reefs for nearly a year and a half, assessing oyster coverage, quantity, and size to gauge how quickly the reef grew. They also deployed water pressure sensors to the newly installed reef and to reference sites without reefs to track wave activity. These sensors, which measure the motion of waves at different locations, were used to determine if the oyster reef created less energy for the coast. Monitoring occurred at several time points after the reef’s construction.They also found that wave energy at the reefs was 40% lower than at the control sites. This indicated that even smaller, younger oyster structures can have an impact on the riverbed and offer protection to the exposed river banks. These results, published in NOAA, provide empirical data on the benefits of oyster restoration. These findings also align with the research published in Ecological Applications, which examines oyster populations living along the shorelines of the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. The research highlights how these structures can reduce wave impacts, even though their effectiveness depends on local environmental conditions and reef design.Why oyster reefs could benefit coastal environments Oyster reefs provide benefits from their ability to slow down waves. As they grow, oysters form dense colonies that produce a rough surface to deflect incoming waves, decreasing the energy that reaches the shore and exposed sediments, which may help reduce erosion along the shoreline. They also provide habitat for fish, crabs, and other marine life. As filter feeders, oysters extract suspended particles from the water column while feeding, and this can have a positive impact on water quality and marine life in the area.One other interesting aspect of this project is its connection with the marsh vegetation. As wave action decreases, marshy plants may find it easier to take hold, which further strengthens the sediment and helps protect the shoreline from deterioration. Ultimately, the effect of the reclaimed structure depends on whether the oysters survive, how fast the reef grows, and other aspects of the water conditions. Effects such as salinity, water depth, tidal cycle, and movement of sediment influence how well the restored structures thrive. These 18-month results are promising, but more monitoring is required to assess whether these positive results persist in the long term.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
articles.summary: Zookeepers say she cannot have surgery but are providing fluids and supportive care to help her pass the hat.
articles.body:
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.

The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".

But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.

Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.

The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.

"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update.

Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January.

At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

articles.title: Arizona parents whose son was diagnosed with a rare genetic disease that could take away his eyesight have now committed $7.1 million to research, offering new hope for restoring vision
articles.summary: An Arizona couple whose son was diagnosed with a rare genetic condition that causes progressive vision loss have now directed $7.1 million towards
articles.body: An Arizona couple whose son was diagnosed with a rare genetic condition that causes progressive vision loss have now directed $7.1 million towards research into inherited retinal diseases. Dr Stephen Johnston and his wife, Kristina Johnston, founded the nonprofit organisation A Race Against Blindness after their son Luke was diagnosed with Bardet-Biedl syndrome in 2020. What began as a family’s effort to find a treatment for their child has since grown into a wider research-funding mission, supporting both gene-specific and gene-agnostic approaches to tackling inherited blindness. The organisation announced its latest $1 million commitment in November 2026, taking its total research grants to $7.1 million, all of which it says has been paid out.A son's rare eye disease inspires parents' $7.1 million missionBardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) is a rare genetic disorder that can affect several parts of the body, including the eyes. In Luke’s case, the condition caused retinitis pigmentosa (RP), a group of inherited retinal disorders in which light-sensitive cells in the retina gradually deteriorate. Vision loss can begin with difficulty seeing in low light and progress to a reduction in peripheral vision, potentially leading to severe visual impairment.The Johnstons said they were told there was little that could be done for their son’s condition. Rather than accept that as the end of the search for answers, they decided to help fund research into possible treatments. They established A Race Against Blindness in 2023, turning their family’s experience into an effort to support children and families affected by inherited retinal diseases.How the $7.1 million will support researchThe organisation’s latest commitment, announced on November 17, 2026, is a $1 million grant made in partnership with the Foundation Fighting Blindness. The money has been divided between two research initiatives:$700,000 to the Gund Vision Fund: The amount will be matched dollar for dollar by the Gordon and Llura Gund Foundation Challenge, taking the total support for the fund to $1.4 million. It will back several gene-agnostic approaches, including research into protecting retinal cells, restoring light sensitivity and developing cell therapies.$300,000 for research led by Dr Jin Woo Kim at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST): The funding will support preclinical work investigating whether the retina's own cells can be encouraged to regenerate.The latest grant follows an earlier $1 million commitment in June 2026, also made through the Foundation Fighting Blindness and the Gund Vision Fund. That funding included $775,000 for the fund, which was matched to $1.55 million, and $225,000 for research led by Dr Thomas Mendel at The Ohio State University.Research aims to help the retina regenerateOne of the projects receiving the latest funding focuses on a protein called PROX1. Dr Kim’s research examines how this protein affects Müller glia, support cells in the retina that have the potential to develop into new retinal cells under certain conditions.A study published in Nature Communications on March 25, 2025, found that PROX1 can restrict the regenerative potential of these cells. Researchers reported that blocking the transfer of PROX1 between retinal cells allowed Müller glia to reprogramme into retinal progenitor cells in injured mouse retinas. In experiments involving mice with retinitis pigmentosa, an antibody designed to block PROX1 promoted the regeneration of retinal neurons and delayed vision loss.The findings offer a possible direction for future treatments, but the research is still at the preclinical stage. The latest funding is intended to help refine the antibody and its delivery, with further studies, including large-animal research, needed before the approach could be considered for human trials. It is not an established treatment for people with inherited retinal diseases.$5.1 million directed towards a gene therapy for Luke's conditionBefore expanding its focus to treatments that could benefit people with different inherited retinal diseases, A Race Against Blindness had concentrated on finding a therapy for the specific genetic condition affecting Luke.The organisation provided $5.1 million to support the development of AXV-101, an experimental gene therapy designed for retinal degeneration associated with mutations in the BBS1 gene. The funding supported work including manufacturing, safety studies and the steps required to move the treatment into clinical testing.The therapy has now entered a first-in-human clinical trial, designed to assess its preliminary safety and tolerability in children with BBS1-related retinal degeneration. The early-stage study is expected to enrol up to 12 participants aged between four and 17. It is an important research milestone, but the trial is not yet evidence that the therapy can restore eyesight.From a family fundraiser to a wider research missionThe Johnstons established A Race Against Blindness in 2023, with their own fundraising efforts helping launch the organisation. One of its early initiatives involved donating a custom adventure van as a sweepstakes prize to raise money for research.Since then, the nonprofit has expanded its support beyond BBS1-related treatments to include approaches that could potentially help people with several forms of inherited retinal disease. According to its published grant record, its $7.1 million in research funding comprises $5.1 million for AXV-101 and another $2 million for gene-agnostic research through the Foundation Fighting Blindness and its Gund Vision Fund.You use AI every day. articles.title: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences
articles.summary: The 83-year-old singer is accused of abusing two former employees at Caribbean residences in 2021.
articles.body:
Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members

Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.

The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.

Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations .

But in a statement published on Wednesday (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.

He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after the he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".

Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.

The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.

In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.

The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario and television network Univision news, published in January.

In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.

The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.

Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.

In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said : "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".

WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.

But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".

The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.

Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.

He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

articles.title: Birmingham City Council wins legal fight over flags on lamp-posts
articles.summary: The decision has been made this afternoon by the High Court in Birmingham.
articles.body:
Birmingham City Council has won a High Court bid to prevent unauthorised flags being put up after a legal battle with campaigners from an anti-migrant group.

The local authority had sought an injunction against members of the group Raise the Colours, who have placed thousands of St George and Union flags on lamp-posts since the summer of 2025. Supporters of the group protested outside the court, wearing Raise the Colours shirts and hoodies.

The council's lawyers said the flags were a road safety risk and created tensions, but supporters argued an order would breach the European Convention on Human Rights.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

The judgment grants the local authority an interim injunction against Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning the police could arrest someone immediately without a warrant if they reasonably suspect the order has been breached.

In her adjudication, Kelly said: "The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is. It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the Union Jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.

"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."

She added that she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

Addressing concerns that had previously been raised by Raise the Colours and their supporters, Kelly said: "Whilst I recognise the genuine anxiety that this application has brought to the interested parties, their concerns that their ability to express themselves will be unduly restricted are unwarranted."

The application had sought to prevent all flags being flown without council permission on street furniture unlawfully, including Palestinian and Pride flags.

Jonathan Manning, representing the authority at the city's High Court hearing, said people in the city had reported feeling "significantly less safe" following a series of "violent and threatening incidents".

The local authority had said the flags could pose "safety risks, obstruct visibility and interfere with highway assets" as well as "contribute to tensions and disorder".

Representing Bridge, barrister Liam Wells had argued the council had failed to prove his client had acted unlawfully and it had not met the legal threshold required to secure an interim injunction.

He told the court at a previous hearing that the flag campaign was an expression of political views protected under Articles 10 and 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which cover freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.

Wells had told the court the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on the expression of Bridge's rights.

Birmingham City councillor Jane Baston, cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, said the local authority was grateful for the granting of the injunction, calling it an "important step to help us address the unauthorised attachments on our public highways".

She also stated that residents remained free to display flags on their own properties.

"We have taken a proportionate and evidence-led approach throughout this case," she said.

"Our priority has always been to protect public safety, supporting the welfare of our staff and contractors, maintaining community cohesion and ensuring public funds are used responsibly.

"I would like to thank residents and community groups for their cooperation and understanding throughout this process."

articles.title: World Bank official says Lebanon reconstruction making slow progress
articles.summary: Beirut blames Israel’s occupation and attacks on southern Lebanon for reconstruction delays.
articles.body:
A senior World Bank official says Lebanon has been slow to use international aid to rebuild areas destroyed during the 2024 war and the renewed fighting since March 2026.

World Bank managing director of operations Anna Bjerde said she had to be “honest” about the pace of reconstruction during a visit to southern Lebanon on Tuesday.

The international financial institution approved $250m in June 2025 to help Lebanon clear rubble and repair “damaged critical public infrastructure” after the 2024 Israel-Hezbollah war. But a September progress report showed that only $4.2m had been paid out, a fraction of the projected $100m by July 2026.

The World Bank estimated that rebuilding after the 2024 war would cost about $11b.

“Parliament ratification of the said loan experienced considerable delays,” Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s office responded in a statement, adding that the “worsening security situation” as a result of Israel’s continuing occupation of southern Lebanon “delayed the timely launch of project activities”.

Israel has continued to occupy and attack parts of southern Lebanon up to the Litani River since March, claiming to destroy Hezbollah infrastructure, while demolishing civilian homes.

On Wednesday, Israel fired artillery shells towards the towns of Baraachit and Beit Yahoun in the Bint Jbeil district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA). The towns of Rashaf and Sarbine, extending to Wadi al-Hujair, were also targeted. And Israeli earth movers demolished residential homes in the town of Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah and Haddatha.

The United Nations estimates at least 304,500 Lebanese remain internally displaced in the country, down from 1.2 million. Up to 4,500 have been killed in Israeli attacks.

Last month, Hezbollah announced it will pay up to $14,000 to families whose homes were destroyed or made uninhabitable by Israel, as the group accused the government of failing to carry out its duties to help the displaced.

Israel has refused to withdraw from southern Lebanon, citing security concerns connected to the delayed disarmament of Hezbollah and other groups, which the United States and the Lebanese government have insisted on, as part of the trilateral ceasefire framework launched in April.

“Israel will not withdraw from the current lines of these security zones, nor will it redeploy its forces,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that if tensions escalate on the various fronts, “we are fully prepared to seize additional territory”.

Bjerde said that “institutions in Lebanon are very thinly stretched” and the security situation required “very careful planning around where you can start and where you don’t start” to remove rubble and repair infrastructure.

The World Bank projected Lebanon’s economy to shrink by 6.4 percent this year , in its Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor report, titled A Conflict-Torn Economy.

“The rebound was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the report said.

According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme, and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than one million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of hunger.

Despite this, Lebanon’s western-backed government insists it is doing all it can, given the circumstances, such as the distribution of approximately $100m in housing loans granted to 1,500 families, according to NNA.

Bjerde said the World Bank needs to be “insistent” and “very close to monitoring on a daily basis” to make sure the work gets done “because you cannot let the people down”, adding that the World Bank wants to see the reconstruction work go more quickly.

articles.title: Railway vents launched to ease flooding at Bengaluru’s Sai Layout, Hennur
articles.summary: Bengaluru adds two railway vents at Geddalahalli to ease flooding in Sai Layout, Hennur and HBR Layout; Rs 16 crore project inaugurated by DK Shivakumar.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Residents of Sai Layout, Hennur, HBR Layout and surrounding areas, which have repeatedly faced flooding during heavy rain, can expect some relief with the completion of two additional railway vents beneath the Geddalahalli intersection.The new infrastructure is expected to improve the flow of rainwater through the Hennur rajakaluve and reduce the risk of water backing up and flooding nearby localities.The narrow railway crossing was a major bottleneck in the drain, restricting the discharge of large volumes of rainwater. This resulted in water overflowing into surrounding residential areas. The two additional vents have been constructed to increase the drainage capacity.Chief minister DK Shivakumar inaugurated the facility Wednesday, even though the construction work was completed in June.Undertaken in collaboration with the railways, the project was executed at a cost of Rs 16 crore. Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) paid Rs 3 crore to the railways towards permission charges.The two new additional vents, each measuring 6 metres in width, 5 metres in depth and 32 metres in length, will carry rainwater flowing from Hebbal Lake, Yelahanka Lake and various parts of the Sarvagnanagar assembly constituency, including the Manyata Tech Park area. By improving the flow at the railway crossing, the project is expected to reduce water stagnation and flooding in Sai Layout, Geddalahalli and neighbouring localities.Despite the completion of the infrastructure, regular desilting and removal of weeds in the drain remain slow. Workers were seen clearing garbage and weeds in the vicinity of the old vents on the day of the inauguration.Meanwhile, Shivakumar also inaugurated the Jakkur railway overbridge and laid the foundation stone for a rotary flyover at IOC Junction near Baiyappanahalli.At the inauguration of the Jakkur railway overbridge, Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda criticised the previous BJP govt for failing to move the project forward. “For four years before our govt came to power, no work progressed. articles.title: AP high court pulls up officials over idol works in Narsipatnam lake despite stay
articles.summary: AP High Court questions officials over ongoing Shiva-Parvati idol construction in Narsipatnam Pedda Cheruvu despite stay; directs counters in contempt plea.
articles.body: Vijayawada: Andhra Pradesh high court on Wednesday questioned officials as to how construction of a Shiva-Parvati idol project was continuing in Narsipatnam’s Pedda Cheruvu despite its April 1 interim order restraining such activity. The court directed authorities and assembly Speaker Chintakayala Ayyannapatrudu, who is also a party respondent in the matter, to file counters in the contempt petition.A division bench comprising Chief Justice Lisa Gill and Justice Challa Gunaranjan said it had clearly barred construction of the idol structure in the lake and asked why the order was not being implemented. The bench rejected the contention that the works were part of lake conservation measures, stressing that water bodies must be protected and natural resources cannot be disturbed in the name of development. The bench further observed that water bodies do not need any protection unless humans damage them.The contempt plea was filed by former Narsipatnam YSRCP MLA Petla Uma Shankar Ganesh, who alleged that construction linked to the proposed Shiva-Parvati idol installation was continuing in violation of the high court’s directions. Earlier, he filed a PIL challenging the ‘Srushti Kshetram’ project in Pedda Cheruvu and sought removal of alleged encroachments.Appearing for the petitioner, senior advocate Ponnavolu Sudhakar Reddy told the court that works were being carried out in the middle of the lake despite the stay and that permissions for the project were granted on the very day the high court passed its interim order.The bench sought clarification from the state on whether idol structures could be permitted within water bodies. Special govt pleader S Pranathi argued that the proposed works would not affect the lake’s extent or storage capacity and that there was no legal bar on such construction. She sought time to place the updated facts before the court.Counsel VV Satish, appearing for Ayyannapatrudu, argued that the PIL was politically motivated and maintained that the project formed part of developmental and conservation works being undertaken in the lake. articles.title: From Dunfermline to Dubai - McPake on new life in Middle East
articles.summary: James McPake has left Scottish football behind for the time being, plying his trade in coaching in Dubai.
articles.body:
James McPake may not have given up on football management but the former Dundee and Dunfermline Athletic boss is discovering there is life beyond the dugout.

Four months after moving to Dubai with his family, the 41-year-old has settled into a new role working in schools to develop young players.

It is a considerable change from the pressures of Scottish football but one that McPake and his family had been contemplating for more than a year.

His wife Dawn, a teacher, secured a position in Dubai before McPake landed his own opportunity, one that has opened up a different world of opportunities, including working alongside some recognisable names in football.

"It's certainly a bit different from back home but we're enjoying it," he says. "There is obviously a big demand for British curriculum teachers, so Dawn managed to get a position and I've been pretty fortunate to land here."

The timing of the family's move has inevitably attracted attention, given the wider tensions in the Middle East and concerns about security in the region.

However, McPake insists their experience of living in Dubai has been very different from some of the headlines.

"You don't hear a lot about it and you don't see anything. It is very much business as usual," he explains. "It's as busy as when we've come here on holiday. It's just like being anywhere else.

"The girls are enjoying it. They feel safe, they enjoy school and they can go out and play at night. We've had no issues that I've seen."

McPake's decision to head overseas has also provided an opportunity to step away from the demands of management and concentrate on developing players.

His responsibilities include overseeing under-16 and under-19 programmes at an impressive set-up, with school timetables adapted to accommodate training and facilities including strength and conditioning rooms, pools and pitches.

"The programme is relatively new but it's similar to the way you would look at an SFA performance school," he says. "The facilities are fantastic. It's difficult not to make a difference when you have facilities like these."

Former Real Madrid and Wales star Gareth Bale recently spent time at the school, answering questions from senior pupils during an hour-long session. And ex- England midfielder Jonjo Shelvey is also working full-time with McPake.

"For the kids, it was a fantastic experience," the former Livingston and Hibernian defender says.

"Gareth sat with myself and the head director of sport and answered question after question. Afterwards, we saw him out on the pitch with some of the younger kids, and Jonjo was on one of our other pitches.

"It's brilliant for the youngsters to have that sort of access to people who have played at the highest level."

McPake's departure from Scotland came at a time when opportunities were becoming increasingly difficult to secure. He admits that was a consideration in the move but not the driving force behind the family's decision.

There remains an obvious desire to return to the dugout but for now he is happy to embrace a different challenge.

"We've always wanted to give this a go, particularly for the girls. We wanted them to have an experience of a different society and culture and broaden their eyes to the world while they were still young," he says.

"The lack of opportunities in Scotland didn't make the decision for us but it certainly didn't cause us any hesitation when we were looking at coming out here.

"We've now been here for a few months, we're settled and we're used to life out here. It's been excellent and better than we imagined."

'No bitterness towards Dundee and Dunfermline'

Although he is now thousands of miles away, McPake continues to follow Scottish football closely, particularly the fortunes of two clubs where he managed.

Dundee, where he was in charge between 2019 and 2022, have impressed him under Steven Pressley. And he also retains an affection for Dunfermline, where he won the League 1 title.

There is particular pride in watching youngsters he helped introduce to senior football begin to make their mark at a higher level.

"Luke Graham getting his first start for Scotland the other night was fantastic. He's a great kid and, even when he was really young and training with us at Dundee, you could see he was going to be the next one," says McPake, who played once for Northern Ireland.

McPake also keeps an eye on the progress of Dunfermline's Tod brothers, Andrew and Jon, who have both progressed through the Scotland international age groups.

There is also no lingering resentment towards either Dundee or Dunfermline, despite the manner in which his managerial spells ended.

McPake acknowledges that losing a job hurts but insists the affection he has for both clubs remains.

"At Dundee, it was excellent," he adds. "I have no bitterness towards them and Dunfermline is the same. We felt we weren't quite backed there.

"Should we have done better? Yes. But we won a very strong League 1 and then they just didn't push on in the Championship."
